title: Curse
intro: Curse begins with feeling becoming speech and ends by asking for the questions to stop. In between, deprivation is converted into potential creative wealth, while an imagined comfortable observer judges the expression of pain as excessive. That judgement becomes a constricting voice the speaker carries around. The later dirty hands and confession introduce implication without naming an offence. He cannot simply speak himself clean: the receiving listener disappears, and forward motion remains an obligation rather than a release.
reading: Hardship as usable artistic material does not remove need; imagined judgement inhibits speech and confession finds no receiver.

revisions.t45-n1: The empty cooking pot names deprivation before the line converts the worries it produces into potential wealth. That is a resourceful description of making material from experience, but also an uncomfortable bargain. A song may gain something from a hardship that the person living it still needs to escape. The following fear of appearing self-pitying adds another demand: use the pain, but do not express it in a way that inconveniences a comfortable listener.
revisions.t45-n3: The anticipated judgement arrives before he has said much. It acts as an internal editor, limiting expression in advance. The next figure is a happy miser, someone imagined to possess the security and distance required to look down on the complaint. That contrast is more specific than a general fear of criticism: one person's comfort becomes the position from which another person's account of need can be dismissed as a performance.
revisions.t45-n2: The familiar headband spell in Journey to the West makes another person's repeated words into bodily coercion. Here nagging leads directly into the image. The voice no longer needs to remain outside the speaker; it can be carried on his head as pressure. That gives the title a continuing mechanism rather than a single malicious sentence: remembered judgement can constrain what he says even when no critic is physically present.
revisions.t45-phrase-confess-air: Turning oneself in normally requires an authority able to receive the admission. Empty air removes that possibility, so the gesture cannot produce a verdict or absolution. The hands that will not wash clean make the desire for release visible, but no specific offence is supplied. The song ends by restricting questions rather than answering them. Its subject is the burden of implication and failed disclosure, not a recoverable crime report.
